title: The Two Pans
stake: The low table needs a fine batch now. The cart crew can use coarser meal if they know which pan it came from.
knowledgeQuestion: What can a result mean when we change the opening of a test?
preview: Two identical practice scoops contain twelve marked bits each. The small pan is for finer meal. The cart can take a mixed pan with its trial slip. There is one tray to send before the bell.

trials.label: the open sifting frame
trials.action: Shake a scoop through the wider openings.
trials.preview: The marked scoop sits over the wider mesh. The tray beneath is empty.
trials.result: Nine marked bits fall through. Three stay on the mesh. This pan includes fine and middle-sized bits.

trials.label: the close sifting frame
trials.action: Shake the matching scoop through the finer openings.
trials.preview: The other scoop starts with the same twelve marked bits. The mesh is tighter.
trials.result: Five bits fall through and seven stay above. The small pan has the finer fraction. Both scoops began with the same mix. Only the mesh changed.

branches.choice: Send the finer pan to the low table.
branches.delivery: the small pan at the low kitchen table
branches.opening: The cook checks the tray with one finger. “Five pieces through the fine mesh. Good. I can start the small smooth batch here.”
branches.action: Set the fine pan beside the small mixing bowl.
branches.result: The low table serves its batch first. The coarse meal remains separate for a later cart. The cook pins the mesh used beside the pan.

branches.choice: Tag the wider-mesh pan for the cart.
branches.delivery: the labelled mixed pan at the loading rail
branches.opening: The loader sets a scoop beside the cart. “This goes farther. I can see why its texture differs from the small pan.”
branches.action: Latch the tray and clip the wider-mesh slip to it.
branches.result: The cart takes nine marked parts. The low table waits for its finer batch. The loader can read which mesh made this pan without reopening the shed.

journal: Both scoops began alike. The mesh and the purpose of the receiving job explain why the pans travelled differently.

object.title: Sifting Basket
object.dimensions: Overall: 39.4 cm (15 1/2 in.); Outside: 39.4 x 20.7 cm (15 1/2 x 8 1/8 in.)
object.place: Democratic Republic of the Congo or Angola
object.observation: The museum identifies a sifting basket woven from plant fibers, with a diameter of 39.4 cm. Its description explains the separation of fine maize flour from coarser particles.
object.limit: The cultural attribution is tentative. The mesh opening and yield are open questions for this basket.
object.dateKind: Latest date of making recorded by the museum
object.altText: Museum view of a woven basket with a round rim and interlaced plant fibers.

title: The Wood Look
stake: A display seller wants to catch a passer’s eye. A repair learner needs a material note they can use at a bench.
knowledgeQuestion: When does a good resemblance stop helping us identify a material?
preview: The catalogue calls the Kuba-style bowl earthenware. These two practice bodies share a profile and a dark finish. Vera needs an honest way to show the resemblance without sending a repair learner to the wood shelf.
arrangeLabel: Vera’s two bowls and the display hooks

trials.label: the matched profiles under the angled lamp
trials.action: Turn both profiles toward the same light.
trials.preview: Both practice rims have the same line. The side lamp lights the upper edges equally.
trials.result: The black finish and cut lines look close from this angle. At the lip, even the grain-like marks could belong to either practice piece.

trials.label: the bare bases and intake slips
trials.action: Turn the two practice bodies over and match the base tags.
trials.preview: The bases are unfinished. Each practice body has a separate maker’s slip under it.
trials.result: One base shows end grain and the tag says wood. The other shows bare clay and a clay tag. The matched lip was a poor material test.

branches.choice: Hang the two look-alike profiles at the display stall with the material note.
branches.delivery: the finished profiles at the display stall
branches.opening: The stall holder points at the two dark rims. “I can start with the surprise. Will you hang the tags where a visitor can turn them?”
branches.action: Clip the two material tags beneath the matched profiles.
branches.result: The display makes the resemblance easy to see from the lane. At the repair bench, a learner still has to request the bare bases before trying a repair.

branches.choice: Take the bare-base pair to the repair learner.
branches.delivery: the identified bases at the repair lane
branches.opening: The learner clears a seat at the bench. “Show me the plain bases. I had already fetched the wood tool for both.”
branches.action: Set each bare base above its own intake slip.
branches.result: The learner can choose a material-specific practice repair. The display lane keeps a small outline card and sends visitors here for the full comparison.

journal: The Kuba-style museum bowl has a documented material and a probable use. The repair pair made the limits of appearance visible without testing the historical bowl.

object.title: Bowl
object.displayName: Kuba-style earthenware bowl with a woodlike surface
object.dimensions: Diameter: 26.4 cm (10 3/8 in.); Overall: 8.4 cm (3 5/16 in.)
object.observation: Earthenware with a surface worked to resemble carved wood. The museum suggests it may once have held cosmetics.
object.limit: The material is documented. The cosmetic use is a curatorial inference.
object.dateKind: Period of making assigned by the museum
object.altText: Museum view of a patterned earthenware bowl with a shallow body and dark surface.

title: The Cover Between Turns
stake: A serving counter needs quick turns. The waiting bench needs a cover that stays in place while the porter is away.
knowledgeQuestion: How do two ways to test a useful feature change what we mean by better?
preview: The Zulu pot record shows a terracotta body and a separate plant-fiber lid. Here the crew has two plain practice water pots, a woven cover and six paper flecks. They can spare the cover for one station.
arrangeLabel: the water pots’ one spare cover

trials.label: the open water pot by the paper fan
trials.action: Leave the first pot open for one fan turn.
trials.preview: Six paper flecks wait on a line. This pot’s opening stays uncovered.
trials.result: Three flecks land in the open pot. When the porter returns, the handle is immediately ready, but the water must be checked before serving.

trials.label: the covered pot by its marked rest
trials.action: Put the woven cover on for the same fan turn.
trials.preview: The second pot is the same size. Six flecks start on the same marks.
trials.result: The woven cover catches the three flecks that reached the opening. When it is lifted, one hand holds the cover and the other reaches the handle.

branches.choice: Station the cover at the serving counter with a lifting rest.
branches.delivery: the busy serving counter and its lifting rest
branches.opening: The server has another cup ready. “When I lift with my left hand, set the cover where I can reach it on the next turn.”
branches.action: Set the cover in the rest between servings.
branches.result: The server can lift and replace the cover in one place. The waiting bench keeps its own smaller vessel until the shared cover returns.

branches.choice: Leave the pot covered at the waiting bench.
branches.delivery: the covered pot on the waiting bench
branches.opening: The porter sets both hands on the loaded crate. “I can put this down before I lift anything. Let the cover stay while I’m out.”
branches.action: Seat the cover and mark the waiting place.
branches.result: The returning porter finds the protected pot ready for a check. The serving counter must pause to bring out a second vessel when its line gets longer.

journal: The fan trials showed what the cover prevents and what the lift costs. The delivery choice used both results.

object.title: Lidded Pot
object.displayName: Zulu terracotta pot and woven lid
object.dimensions: Diameter: 45.7 cm (18 in.); Overall: 33 cm (13 in.)
object.attribution: Zulu attribution, potter and lid maker individually unrecorded
object.observation: The record catalogues a terracotta vessel and plant-fiber lid together. The museum says the lid helps keep debris out of the opening.
object.limit: The catalogue associates the historic vessel with beer service. The game trial uses water and independent plain model covers.
object.dateKind: Century of making recorded by the museum
object.altText: Museum view of a rounded lidded pot. The catalogue identifies a separate plant-fiber lid.

title: Where the Fleck Stopped
stake: Two water stall keepers need different things from one test. One needs a quick catch tray. The other needs a way to repeat the check.
knowledgeQuestion: What can a successful model tell us about the purpose of an older object?
preview: The Smithsonian identifies a Ganda artist and describes a loosely woven end that probably served as a filter. Sali has two new clear trial tubes of matching width. One has a plain open end and one has a woven sleeve. Both carry water to paper catch trays.
arrangeLabel: Sali’s tray and two signed sleeve slips

trials.label: the plain tube and catch sheet
trials.action: Release one measure of water through the plain test tube.
trials.preview: The plain tube has no end sleeve. A flat paper fleck floats in the trial water.
trials.result: The fleck reaches the catch sheet with the water. That is the comparison for the same release through the sleeved tube.

trials.label: the sleeved tube and catch sheet
trials.action: Release the second measure through the woven trial sleeve.
trials.preview: The second dose has another fleck of the same size. The sleeve sits across the tube end.
trials.result: The sleeve keeps the fleck at the opening and the water reaches the catch sheet. The trial supports a possible filter use for that shape. It tests this sleeve only.

branches.choice: Fit the removable test sleeve at the wash station and keep its test label.
branches.delivery: the removable trial sleeve at the wash station
branches.opening: The wash keeper holds up a clean sheet. “I can show a worker what this sample sleeve caught. Leave the comparison on the sheet.”
branches.action: Set the sleeved trial and the plain result side by side.
branches.result: A worker can repeat the catch demonstration at the wash station. The historical label keeps “probably served as a filter” with the museum object.

branches.choice: Send both labelled catch sheets to the measure desk.
branches.delivery: both catch sheets at the measure desk
branches.opening: The clerk marks two spaces on the form. “Next time they bring a different sleeve, I’ll need these two results as a pair.”
branches.action: Clip each catch sheet to its tested tube sketch.
branches.result: The desk receives records it can use in a repeat test. The wash station gets only an empty stand until a new sleeve arrives.

journal: The water trial made a possible purpose visible. It gives no direct record of how the late nineteenth-century reed was used.

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
object.title: Beer straw
object.place: Uganda, collected there in 1882 according to the Smithsonian record
object.observation: The catalogue identifies a reed shaft with a plant-fibre surround. It describes a loosely woven bulb-like end that probably acted as a filter.
object.limit: The historic material record gives reed, plant fibre and copper alloy. It calls the filter function probable. The fictional water trial measures what happened in the practice sleeve.
object.dateKind: Period of making recorded by the museum
object.altText: Smithsonian photograph of a narrow curved reed with long woven sections and a wider woven end.

title: The Shuttle’s Path
stake: The loom scene needs a moving part that a performer can repeat. A visitor might miss the second face if the moving frame turns away.
knowledgeQuestion: How can the appearance and movement of a tool answer different questions?
preview: The Met shows a Baule heddle pulley with opposing carved faces. The loft has a plain rig for its play. Two rows of cord cross at the same height, and a flat wooden shuttle waits beside them. Change the pull and see where the gap opens.

trials.label: the first rig pull with both rows even
trials.action: Draw the marked cord to raise the near row.
trials.preview: The shuttle sits at the first tape mark. The far row stays low when you lift the near row.
trials.result: The layers separate. The shuttle passes the first gap and stops on the opposite side. A side-on drawing still shows only one face of the carved reference.

trials.label: the second rig pull at the far hook
trials.action: Ease the near row and pull the far row high.
trials.preview: The shuttle sits at the far tape mark for the return run. This pull opens the other gap.
trials.result: The shuttle can return as the two rows change places. The paired faces belong to the record drawing. The change in the thread belongs to the working rig.

branches.choice: Set the working rig at the near rehearsal rail.
branches.delivery: the moving plain loom rig at the near rail
branches.opening: One performer needs to time the shuttle to the pull. The lower rail places both hand marks within reach.
branches.action: Hook both pull cords on the rehearsal marks.
branches.result: The performer completes a back-and-forth rehearsal without an assistant. Visitors can find the Baule pulley’s name and two faces beside the drawing. The plain working rig carries the prop maker’s own mark.

branches.choice: Set the paired-face drawing out at the high rail.
branches.delivery: the two views of the carved pulley at the high rail
branches.opening: A visitor rotates a drawing over their palm. “Now I can keep both views in sight. Could you leave this open while I trace the cord?”
branches.action: Mount the paired drawing and one working cord sample.
branches.result: The visitor traces the line in a still view. She leaves the Baule attribution with that drawing and uses a separate label for the practice rig. The performers can share their own method without speaking for the pulley’s maker.

journal: The plain rig answered a movement question. The carved Baule pulley’s opposing faces gave visitors a separate reason to look.

object.title: Heddle pulley with opposing faces
object.observation: The wooden heddle pulley has two opposing faces. The Met describes a heddle pulley as a tool that helps the heddles separate the warp on a narrow-band loom.
object.limit: The pulley helps explain the operation of the loom. The maker’s name and this pulley’s users remain open questions.
object.dateKind: Approximate date of making assigned by the museum
object.altText: Met photograph of a tall carved wooden heddle pulley with an attachment opening.

title: The Lintel That Changed
stake: The carpenter needs an entire stage outline, while the gallery reader needs to see where the old profile breaks.
knowledgeQuestion: When may a mismatched piece support a history of change?
preview: The Met describes a Zanzibar door’s lotus from two angles and a top frame that may come from another door. The stage carpenter has drawn a plain invented lintel in two pieces. Trace each edge before masking the seam.
arrangeLabel: the carpenter’s full and split framing papers

trials.label: the face and overhead tracings
trials.action: Line up the front and top outlines using both marks.
trials.preview: A side outline and an overhead one share a centre peg.
trials.result: The two views agree on the centre. One outline shows a raised section that looks flat in the other view. Move your second mark to the outer framing piece.

trials.label: the loose upper framing piece
trials.action: Lift the upper piece and compare the two edge sequences.
trials.preview: The lower model repeats a notch on both sides. The top piece has one offset hole.
trials.result: The notch marks align on the lower piece. The top hole has no matching mark. This practice joint makes a replacement possible without proving a date for the older door.

branches.choice: Hang the whole outline with a broken line marking the join.
branches.delivery: the full outline on the scenery rack
branches.opening: The carpenter has one long measure in hand. A broken line in the whole outline gives them a place to stop before mistaking the top for one piece.
branches.action: Hang the full outline and secure the seam key.
branches.result: The scenery crew can lay their opening out from one view. A visitor following the hypothesis still has to take a second look at the join key.

branches.choice: Set the two framing papers on separate supports with one comparison peg.
branches.delivery: the two framing pieces at the reading bench
branches.opening: The reader puts one finger at the left notch and another at the unmatched hole. “I can compare the pieces if you give me a shared mark.”
branches.action: Set the matching peg beside both framing papers.
branches.result: The reader can see the possible replacement and keep its uncertainty. The scenery crew takes a separate whole-width sketch for measurements.

journal: The trial preserved the whole opening and the possibly replaced section as different questions. The date remained the museum’s qualified estimate.

object.title: Carved door
object.dimensions: H. 270 cm x W. 150 cm x D. 26 cm
object.observation: The Met identifies an upper carving that breaks the symmetry of the rest of the door. It suggests that framing element came from another door. A lotus motif in the lintel shows two views.
object.limit: The replacement is a curatorial interpretation. The original household and the date of each component remain open questions.
object.dateKind: Likely period of making based on stylistic comparison in the catalogue
object.altText: Met photograph of a tall carved timber door with a central joint, decorated frame and brass fittings.

title: The Pattern Below the Seat
stake: The usher needs a clear seat profile for readers. The lighting crew needs a way to show the openings underneath without naming every shape.
knowledgeQuestion: How does our viewing position affect what a pattern can support?
preview: The Met assigns this carved seat to a Duala artist. The open carving sits below a curved top. Here there is a plain practice frame with an open underside. Move one light between its two fixed marks and let the viewers see what changes.
arrangeLabel: the lighting crew’s shadow and outline carriers

trials.label: the front lamp at the seat outline
trials.action: Set the lamp level with the upper edge.
trials.preview: The practice frame rests on the white board. The lamp can be held level with its top.
trials.result: Both edges of the upper curve show clearly. Most of the openings underneath merge into one band in the flat shadow.

trials.label: the lower lamp at the open underside
trials.action: Drop the lamp to the low mark and trace the openings.
trials.preview: The same frame stays on the board. The lower mark lights between the pieces.
trials.result: The separate openings are now visible. The top looks flatter from this position. The two light positions give two views of the same setup.

branches.choice: Leave the seating outline at the entry instructions.
branches.delivery: the seat profile by the usher’s low mark
branches.opening: The usher checks the drawing from the entry mark. “The upper edge shows here. I can point to it without crowding a waiting visitor.”
branches.action: Clip the outline at seated eye level.
branches.result: The entrance can use the outline for the demonstration. The lamp crew retains the side notes, so this carrier leaves the open carving for a later view.

branches.choice: Give the separate openings to the side-light crew.
branches.delivery: the opening shadows at the side-light stand
branches.opening: A lamp worker holds the low trace against a screen. They can see three spaces, but one still looks joined from the back row.
branches.action: Fix the trace beside the lamp’s viewpoint mark.
branches.result: The side-light crew can repeat the view and explain which mark a reader used. The usher keeps the plain outline for the doorway.

journal: The two lights changed the visible pattern. The catalogue’s stylistic reading stayed with the specific Duala seat.

object.title: Prestige seat
object.displayName: Duala seat with a carved lattice
object.observation: The wooden seat has a curving upper surface and open latticework below. The Met places it in a small group of nineteenth-century seats for prominent elders.
object.limit: The gallery proposes one reading of the animal shape. The owner’s name and the exact reading of the imagery are open questions.
object.dateKind: Period of making assigned by the museum
object.altText: Met photograph of a wooden seat with a curved top over an open carved lattice.

title: The Place on the Crate
stake: The host needs something readable at the entrance. A research visitor needs enough room for two regional comparisons and a purchase receipt.
knowledgeQuestion: What follows from where an object was bought, and what would need other evidence?
preview: The Met’s cotton-and-wool hanging was bought in Ghana in the 1870s. Its exact origin remains open. Hari has a fictional cloth and a sale tag for a rehearsal display. The cloth has two kinds of marks. Check the hook and the folded comparison sheet before printing the place line.
arrangeLabel: Hari’s short tag and three-panel support

trials.label: the sale tag under the end hook
trials.action: Unfold the tag and match its receipt number.
trials.preview: The tag’s edge is tucked around the pole. A second copy of the number sits in the sale book.
trials.result: Both copies record where the piece changed hands. The line for who made it is blank. A number can join the two sale slips without filling that blank.

trials.label: the hanging’s two comparison strips
trials.action: Let down one fold and compare the strips side by side.
trials.preview: Each sketch marks a join, but their title strips cite different collections. The cloth being tested stays on its own pole.
trials.result: One detail on the cloth resembles the first sketch and another resembles the second. There is no signed making record. The match gives a reader places to investigate.

branches.choice: Put a short purchase tag at the entrance.
branches.delivery: the hanging’s purchase tag at the entrance
branches.opening: A visitor can read a single line before the bell. “Ghana tells me where it was bought. Where can I see the rest?”
branches.action: Face the purchase tag toward the visitor and point to the study copy.
branches.result: The tag serves the entrance queue without assigning an origin. Readers who want to compare weaving move to the research table later.

branches.choice: Mount the purchase receipt and two comparison strips at the long bench.
branches.delivery: the cloth comparison between two readers
branches.opening: Two readers have enough bench space to walk around the hanging sketch. They put the purchase tag down before choosing a comparison.
branches.action: Mount the receipt beside both separate comparison strips.
branches.result: The two readers can follow different leads with the purchase kept in its own place. The entrance keeps a small arrow while it waits for a shorter copy.

journal: The receipt located a purchase. Similarities gave a reader a research lead while the place of making remained open.

object.title: Interior Hanging
object.displayName: Cotton-and-wool interior hanging with an open attribution
object.attribution: Attributed in the catalogue as Mende, Vai, or Temne, maker unrecorded
object.place: Sierra Leone is the catalogue’s geographic association, purchased in Ghana
object.observation: The hanging combines cotton and wool. The Met records a purchase in Ghana in the 1870s and says its exact origin is unresolved.
object.limit: The curator notes similarities with several weaving traditions. The record lists Mende, Vai or Temne as possibilities. Ghana is the recorded place of purchase.
object.dateKind: Period of making assigned by the museum
object.altText: Met photograph of a broad cloth hanging with horizontal patterned bands and narrow joined sections.
